title.en: Thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases

text.en: Railway engineers leave small gaps between rails and the bridge builders leave rollers under one end of a bridge. Without these gaps, the metal would bend in the summer heat because everything expands when it is heated.

When heat energy is given to a substance its temperature may rise, its state may change and it expands; all solids, liquids and gases undergo thermal expansion.
In linear expansion the length changes; the coefficient of linear expansion is the increase in length per unit length per degree rise in temperature, and its SI unit is per kelvin.
The change in length is given by delta L = alpha L zero delta T, where delta T is the final minus the initial temperature.
In superficial or areal expansion the area increases, and delta A = alpha A times A zero times delta T, with its own coefficient of superficial expansion.
In cubical expansion the volume increases, and delta V = alpha V times V zero times delta T, with the coefficient of cubical expansion measured in per kelvin.
Different materials have different coefficients; for example water is about 20.7 times 10 to the power minus 5 and mercury is 18.2 times 10 to the power minus 5 per kelvin while glass is only 2.5 times 10 to the power minus 5.
For the same rise in temperature a liquid expands more than a solid and a gas expands the most.
A liquid must be heated in a container, which also expands, so the level we see rising is only the apparent expansion.
Real expansion is the true expansion of the liquid; real expansion is always more than the apparent expansion, because the container also expands.
Real expansion equals apparent expansion plus the expansion of the container, which is why a thermometer bulb first dips slightly when placed in hot water.

problem.en: A steel rail is 30 m long at 20 degrees Celsius. Its coefficient of linear expansion is 1.2 x 10^-5 per kelvin. Find the increase in length when the temperature rises to 50 degrees Celsius.

text.en: delta L = alpha L0 delta T = 1.2 x 10^-5 x 30 x 30.
So the final length is 30.0108 m; engineers leave a gap of at least this much.

prompt.en: Why does the level of a liquid in a glass vessel first fall a little and then rise when the vessel is heated?

requiredIdeas.en: The container is heated first and expands, so the level falls
Then the liquid receives heat and expands more than the container
Real expansion is more than the apparent expansion

commonMisconceptions.en: Heat first makes the liquid contract

points.en: Expansion happens in solids, liquids and gases; gases expand most.
